# bauhaus <img src="man/figures/logo.png" align="right" height="138" alt="" />

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/ashgreat/bauhaus-clock-ggplot/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/ashgreat/bauhaus-clock-ggplot/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![pkgdown](https://github.com/ashgreat/bauhaus-clock-ggplot/actions/workflows/pkgdown.yaml/badge.svg)](https://ashgreat.github.io/bauhaus-clock-ggplot/)
<!-- badges: end -->

**ggplot2 themes from the dials of the Bauhaus Clock screensaver.**

bauhaus brings the sixteen day dials of the Bauhaus Clock macOS screensaver to ggplot2. Every theme
paints the plot on the dial's paper plate, complete with the screensaver's fine paper grain, sets
type in the screensaver's typeface, and takes its text, grid, geom and palette colours from the
inks, steel, lume and shadow tints measured on that dial.

```{r dials, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 8, dpi = 120}
clocks <- lapply(bauhaus_dial_names(), bauhaus_clock, minute_numerals = FALSE)
wrap_plots(clocks, ncol = 4) &
  theme(plot.margin = margin(1.5, 1.5, 1.5, 1.5))
```

<sup>All sixteen dials, drawn with `bauhaus_clock()`.</sup>

* **Sixteen themes**: White, Turquoise, Glacier, Ocean, Tennis, Signal Blue, Salmon, Yellow, Beige,
  Pistachio, Lavender, Rose, Sky Blue, Cream, Slate and Noir. Only the day dials are included.
* **The screensaver's paper grain**, generated with the same algorithm, kernel and seed, at the
  strength measured for each dial.
* **The screensaver's typeface**, Zalando Sans Expanded, bundled and registered automatically.
* **Matching palettes and scales**: an eight-colour discrete palette and a sequential ramp per dial,
  set as the plot's defaults by each theme.
* **The dial itself**: `bauhaus_clock()` draws the clock face, at any time, in any colourway.

See the [website](https://ashgreat.github.io/bauhaus-clock-ggplot/) for a
[gallery](https://ashgreat.github.io/bauhaus-clock-ggplot/articles/gallery.html) of every dial and
the full documentation.

## Installation

bauhaus needs R 4.1 or later and ggplot2 4.0 or later. Install it from GitHub:

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("ashgreat/bauhaus-clock-ggplot")

# or
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ashgreat/bauhaus-clock-ggplot")
```

For the bundled typeface to show up, draw with a device that uses systemfonts, such as
[ragg](https://ragg.r-lib.org) (see [Fonts and devices](#fonts-and-devices)):

```r
install.packages("ragg")
```

## Quick start

Build a plot as usual and add `theme_bauhaus()`. The default dial is Turquoise, the screensaver's
own default.

```{r quick-start, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.4}
library(ggplot2)
library(bauhaus)

penguins <- na.omit(palmerpenguins::penguins)

p <- ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.9) +
  labs(
    title = "Palmer penguins",
    subtitle = "Body mass against flipper length",
    x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", colour = "Species"
  )

p + theme_bauhaus()
```

Pick any other dial by name, or use its shortcut:

```{r quick-start-2, eval = FALSE}
p + theme_bauhaus("ocean")
p + theme_bauhaus("Signal Blue") # case, spaces and underscores don't matter
p + theme_bauhaus_yellow()
```

```{r six, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6.2}
q <- ggplot(penguins, aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.1, alpha = 0.9, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)")
six <- c("ocean", "yellow", "rose", "tennis", "cream", "noir")
plots <- lapply(six, function(d) {
  q + labs(title = bauhaus_dials$name[bauhaus_dials$dial == d]) + theme_bauhaus(d, base_size = 9.5)
})
wrap_plots(plots, ncol = 3) & theme(plot.margin = margin(10, 12, 8, 10))
```

## The sixteen dials

| Dial | Theme | Paper | Numerals | Track | Grain σ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
```{r dial-table, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
d <- bauhaus_dials
cat(sprintf(
  "| %s | `theme_bauhaus(\"%s\")` | `%s` | `%s` | `%s` | %s |\n",
  d$name, d$dial, d$paper, d$numeral, d$track, ifelse(d$grain == 0, "none", as.character(d$grain))
), sep = "")
```

The colours were measured from the screensaver's dial artwork. Plates are defined in Display P3 and
converted to sRGB; the paper is the plate lifted by 13/255, as the screensaver lifts it before adding
the grain. `bauhaus_colours()` returns all twelve colours of a dial, and `bauhaus_dials` has every
dial in one data frame.

```{r colours}
bauhaus_colours("signal_blue")
```

## What a theme sets

`theme_bauhaus()` returns a complete theme, so it replaces whatever theme a plot had. It sets:

* **Background**: the dial's paper with its grain, under the whole plot (panels, legends and strips
  are transparent).
* **Type**: Zalando Sans Expanded for body text and its semibold weight for titles.
* **Ink**: titles, axis titles and the default geom colour use the hour-numeral ink; subtitles,
  captions, axis labels, ticks and grid lines use the minute-track ink, with round line ends like
  the track's ticks. Where the track ink is too faint to read (Cream and Slate), it is pushed towards
  the numeral ink.
* **Palettes**: the dial's discrete palette for discrete colour and fill, its sequential palette for
  continuous colour and fill, and an accent for things like `geom_smooth()`.

So a single theme call gives matching colours throughout:

```{r defaults, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.8}
bars <- ggplot(mpg, aes(y = class, fill = drv)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Cars by class", x = "Count", y = NULL, fill = "Drive") +
  theme_bauhaus("salmon", grid = "x")

heat <- ggplot(faithfuld, aes(waiting, eruptions, fill = density)) +
  geom_raster() +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Old Faithful", x = "Waiting (min)", y = "Eruption (min)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_bauhaus("salmon")

(bars | heat) + plot_annotation(theme = theme_bauhaus("salmon"))
```

Options:

| Argument | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `dial` | `"turquoise"` | Which dial to use. |
| `base_size` | `11` | Base font size in points. |
| `base_family`, `header_family` | Zalando Sans Expanded | Font families for body text and titles. |
| `grain` | `TRUE` | `TRUE` for the dial's measured grain, `FALSE` for a flat plate, or a number for the strength. |
| `grain_density` | `150` | Grain samples per inch. Lower values give a coarser grain. |
| `grid` | `"xy"` | Major grid lines: `"xy"`, `"x"`, `"y"` or `"none"`. |

Set a dial for every plot in a session with `theme_set(theme_bauhaus("pistachio"))`.

## Palettes and scales

Every dial has two palettes:

* **Discrete** (eight colours): the dial's signature colour and ink first, then accents borrowed from
  the other dials (their plates, inks and shadow tints), chosen to stand out against this dial's
  plate.
* **Sequential**: a ramp of the dial's own colours, from the daylight lume (on light dials) or just
  above the plate (on dark dials), through its signature or track colour, to its numeral ink.

```{r palettes, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 7.2}
n <- nrow(d)
rows <- data.frame(dial = d$name, y = rev(seq_len(n)), paper = d$paper, ink = d$numeral)
dots <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
  data.frame(y = rows$y[i], x = 3 + 0:7 * 0.62, colour = bauhaus_palette(d$dial[i]))
}))
ggplot() +
  geom_tile(aes(x = 5.65, y = y, fill = I(paper)), data = rows, width = 11.3, height = 0.94) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 0.15, y = y, label = dial, colour = I(ink)), data = rows, hjust = 0, size = 3.2, family = bauhaus_font_family("semibold")) +
  geom_point(aes(x, y, colour = I(colour)), data = dots, size = 4.6) +
  lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
    ramp <- bauhaus_palette(d$dial[i], type = "sequential", n = 200)
    annotation_raster(matrix(ramp, nrow = 1), xmin = 8.3, xmax = 10.7, ymin = rows$y[i] - 0.21, ymax = rows$y[i] + 0.21)
  }) +
  annotate("text", x = c(3 + 3.5 * 0.62, 9.5), y = n + 0.85, label = c("Discrete", "Sequential"), size = 3.1, family = bauhaus_font_family(), colour = "#004F5D") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 11.3), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.5, n + 1.2), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_grain(fill = bauhaus_colours("turquoise")[["paper"]], colour = NA, sigma = 3.8))
```

Each theme already uses its dial's palettes. Add a scale to borrow another dial's palette, reverse
one, or set other scale arguments:

| Scale | For | Palette |
|---|---|---|
| `scale_colour_bauhaus_d()`, `scale_fill_bauhaus_d()` | discrete data | eight colours |
| `scale_colour_bauhaus_c()`, `scale_fill_bauhaus_c()` | continuous data | sequential ramp |
| `scale_colour_bauhaus_b()`, `scale_fill_bauhaus_b()` | binned data | sequential ramp in steps |

```{r scales, eval = FALSE}
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = class)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_bauhaus_d("ocean") + # Ocean's palette on the Noir dial
  theme_bauhaus("noir")
```

The palettes are also available as colour vectors and palette functions:

```{r palette-vectors}
bauhaus_palette("turquoise")
bauhaus_palette("turquoise", type = "sequential", n = 5)
pal_bauhaus("yellow")(3)
```

## The paper grain

The screensaver's plates are not flat fills; they carry a fine paper grain. bauhaus generates the
same grain, step by step:

1. Uniform white noise from a 32-bit xorshift generator, with the screensaver's seed, fills a
   seamless 512 × 512 tile.
2. A 7 × 5 kernel measured from the original artwork turns it into short horizontal streaks, two to
   three samples long, with no mottling or fibres.
3. The grain is scaled to unit variance, softened at the tails, and added equally to red, green and
   blue at each dial's measured strength: from none on White to 7.8 code values on Tennis.

The themes draw it with `element_grain()`, a rectangle element that works like `element_rect()` and
can be used in any theme. The grain is drawn at a fixed physical size, 150 samples per inch, so it
looks the same on a small figure and a poster.

```{r grain, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
ggplot(mpg, aes(class)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#30475E") +
  labs(title = "Grained paper in any theme", x = NULL, y = "Count") +
  theme_classic(base_family = bauhaus_font_family()) +
  theme(plot.background = element_grain(fill = "#F2EBDD", sigma = 6, colour = NA))
```

The grain is a raster image, which works on every graphics device. It makes PDF and SVG files
larger; `options(bauhaus.grain = FALSE)` draws flat backgrounds everywhere instead.

## Fonts and devices

The package bundles **Zalando Sans Expanded**, the typeface the screensaver's dial numerals are set
in (SIL Open Font License 1.1), and registers it with
[systemfonts](https://systemfonts.r-lib.org) when it loads. Nothing needs installing, as long as the
graphics device uses systemfonts:

* **Files**: `ggsave()` uses ragg for PNG, JPEG and TIFF when ragg is installed, and svglite for
  SVG.
* **R Markdown and Quarto**: set the chunk option `dev = "ragg_png"`.
* **RStudio**: *Tools › Global Options › General › Graphics › Backend: AGG*.
* **Positron**: uses ragg when it is installed.

Other devices don't see the bundled font: `pdf()` falls back to Helvetica and the default Windows
and macOS screen devices to their system sans. To get the real typeface there, call
`bauhaus_showtext()`, which registers the fonts with [showtext](https://github.com/yixuan/showtext)
and turns it on. `bauhaus_font_files()` gives the paths of the font files, if you would rather
install them on your system.

## The dial itself

`bauhaus_clock()` draws the screensaver's dial as a ggplot: the minute track and numerals, steel
hour indices with lume inlays, hour numerals (with the dial's capsule-shaped "1"), and the three
hands with their tinted shadows, on the grained plate. Everything is drawn as shapes, so it scales
to any size.

```{r clock, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4}
bauhaus_clock("turquoise") | bauhaus_clock("noir", time = "16:42:30")
```

## Tips

* **Combining plots**: each plot draws its own background. With
  [patchwork](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com), add
  `plot_annotation(theme = theme_bauhaus("ocean"))` so the space around and between the plots is
  paper too.
* **Saving**: `ggsave()` picks up the paper colour as the background. Use `dpi = 300` for print.
* **Many categories**: the discrete palettes stop at eight colours. Lump the smallest groups
  together, or use a sequential scale for ordered data.
* **Annotations**: take colours from `bauhaus_colours()` and the typeface from
  `bauhaus_font_family()` so labels match the theme.

## Functions

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `theme_bauhaus()`, `theme_bauhaus_<dial>()` | The themes. |
| `scale_colour_bauhaus_d()`, `_c()`, `_b()` and the `fill` versions | Colour scales. |
| `bauhaus_palette()`, `pal_bauhaus()`, `pal_bauhaus_c()` | Palettes as colours and palette functions. |
| `bauhaus_colours()`, `bauhaus_dials`, `bauhaus_dial_names()` | The measured colours. |
| `element_grain()` | The paper grain theme element. |
| `bauhaus_font_family()`, `bauhaus_font_files()`, `bauhaus_showtext()` | The typeface. |
| `bauhaus_clock()` | Draw the dial. |
